summary: Adds the ability for RDAP clients to request partial responses, limiting the amount of information returned, especially for search queries. Without this, servers return everything the client is allowed to see, which wastes resources for both sides.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of getting the whole file when you only need the name and phone number, you can ask for just the pieces you want.

questions: how to limit rdap response fields
what is the rdap fieldset parameter
what are the rdap id brief and full field sets
what does rdap return for an unsupported field set
subtitle: How an RDAP client can ask for a trimmed-down answer instead of every field the server holds.

tldr.problem: RDAP servers can only return full responses with everything the client is allowed to see, which wastes bandwidth and server resources, especially for search queries.
tldr.mechanism: The client adds a fieldSet query parameter naming a server-defined set of fields, and the server may describe its available sets in a subsetting_metadata section of the response.
tldr.outcome: Servers can return smaller answers and apply different limits per field set. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and registers the subsetting extension in the RDAP Extensions registry.

today: RFC 8982 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Partial Responses
sections.content:
Partial responses are common in RESTful API design: rather than returning every data field of each result object, the server returns a subset. The RFC lists the benefits as less data on the network, faster server responses, less CPU time on server and client, and less client memory.

RDAP (the Registration Data Access Protocol) had no such option. Under RFC 7483 a server can only give the client a full response, and it cannot limit what it returns based on the client's preferences. This document adds a query parameter to fix that, using HTTP and the conventions of RFC 7480.
sections.plainLanguage: Right now the server hands you the entire phone book even if you only want one page. This RFC lets you ask for a shorter version.

sections.title: The fieldSet Query Parameter
sections.content:
The RFC defines an OPTIONAL extension of the search path segments from RFC 7482. It introduces one query parameter, fieldSet, whose value is a non-empty string naming a server-defined set of fields that is returned in place of the full response.

An example from the RFC is https://example.com/rdap/domains?name=example*.com&fieldSet=afieldset. Which field sets a server supports is usually described out of band, for example in an RDAP profile. The RFC also defines an in-band way to advertise them.

Appendix A explains why the authors chose named sets over letting the client list individual fields. Field lists need a syntax, are hard to express for nested JSON, require the client to know the data structure, and may ask for fields the client is not authorized to see. Named sets are easier for providers to implement and for clients to request, and predefined sets make it easier to set result limits.
sections.plainLanguage: You do not pick every item yourself. You pick a combo from the menu, like a kids' meal, and the restaurant decides what is in it.

sections.title: Subsetting Metadata
sections.content:
Following REST ideas known as HATEOAS, a client should discover available actions from links the server provides. So servers implementing fieldSet SHOULD describe their field sets in a new JSON structure called subsetting_metadata.

  • currentFieldSet (REQUIRED): the value of the fieldSet parameter, or the default field set that was applied.
  • availableFieldSets (OPTIONAL): an array of objects, each with a name (REQUIRED), a default boolean (REQUIRED), an optional description and optional links.

A server MUST define only one default field set. A server that returns subsetting_metadata MUST include subsetting in the rdapConformance array.

The links array uses Web Linking from RFC 8288 to give ready-made references to each alternative. The value, rel and href members MUST be specified; the rest are OPTIONAL.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can attach a little note to its answer saying which menu it used and what other menus exist, with a link for each one.

sections.title: Basic Field Sets and Relationships
sections.content:
The RFC defines three basic field sets that servers MAY implement: id, brief and full.

  • id returns only the key field: handle for entities and ldhName for domains and nameservers. For an internationalized domain name or nameserver, unicodeName MUST also be included.
  • brief holds the fields suitable for a short response with basic knowledge of each object.
  • full holds all the information the server can provide for an object.

objectClassName is implicitly in every one of these sets. Providers SHOULD include a links field with the self relationship and MAY add service-information properties. Fields in brief and full responses MUST respect the user's access and authorization levels.

For second-level objects, a response may contain no relationships (for an abbreviated set) or associated objects as in a normal RDAP response. Each field set can say how the additional objects are formatted.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three standard menus: just the name tags, a short summary, or everything. Which fields you actually see still depends on what you are allowed to see.

sections.title: Negative Answers
sections.content: A request with an empty or unsupported fieldSet value MUST produce an HTTP 400 (Bad Request) response. The response MAY also carry extra information about supported field sets in the HTTP entity body. The RFC's example uses an error body with errorCode 400, a title saying the field set is not valid, and a description listing the supported sets.
sections.plainLanguage: If you order something that is not on the menu, the server says no and may tell you what it does have.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Search queries typically need more server memory, CPU cycles and bandwidth than lookup queries, which raises the risk of resource exhaustion and denial of service. Partial responses help, combined with other strategies such as restricting search, rate limiting, and truncating and paging results.

Partial responses also let operators enforce data access policy using the HTTP authentication mechanisms of RFC 7481. The fields in each set can differ by client authorization level, and the available sets can be restricted per client. Servers can also set different result limits per field set.
sections.plainLanguage: Smaller answers mean the server is less likely to be overwhelmed, and the server can give trusted people a bigger menu than strangers.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA registered one value in the RDAP Extensions registry. The extension identifier is subsetting, the registry operator is Any, the published specification is RFC 8982, and the contact is the IETF. The intended usage is described as a best practice for partial response provisioning.
sections.plainLanguage: The word subsetting was written in an official list so everyone uses it for the same thing.

items.label: Keys only
items.desc: Only handle for entities, or ldhName for domains and nameservers (plus unicodeName for IDNs).

items.label: Everything
items.desc: All the information the server can provide for the object.
